prompt: What makes a subnet in AWS public?
hint: AWS has no field called private.

choices.text: A route table that sends `0.0.0.0/0` to an internet gateway
choices.why: Right. That route, in the table the subnet follows, is the whole definition.

choices.text: An address range outside the private blocks of RFC 1918
choices.why: Both of the clinic's subnets use private ranges, and one of them is public.

choices.text: A setting chosen in `create-subnet`
choices.why: There is no such option; `create-subnet` takes a range and a zone.

choices.text: The name or tag it was given when it was created
choices.why: A name decides nothing; the routes do.

prompt: `describe-route-tables` filtered by the records subnet's association returned nothing at all. What does that mean?
hint: Every VPC is created with one table already in it.

choices.text: The filter was wrong, since every subnet is explicitly associated with some table
choices.why: Most subnets in real accounts have no explicit association; that is the case the lesson is about.

choices.text: moto lost the association
choices.why: Nobody made one. AWS answers the same way.

choices.text: The subnet has no routes, so it cannot reach anything
choices.why: It still has the local route; it gets it from the main table.

choices.text: The subnet follows the VPC's main route table
choices.why: Right. No explicit association means the main table's routes.

prompt: A VPC has six subnets. Two are associated with a public table, one with a private table, and three with nothing. Someone adds `0.0.0.0/0` to an internet gateway to the main table. How many subnets gained a route to the internet?
hint: Only the ones that follow the main table changed.

choices.text: Three
choices.why: Right. The three unassociated ones; the two public ones already had the route, and the private one follows its own table.

choices.text: None, because a route only applies to the subnet named in it
choices.why: A route names a destination, not a subnet; a table applies to every subnet that follows it.

choices.text: Four: the three with nothing, plus the private one
choices.why: The private one has an explicit association and follows its own table.

choices.text: Six, since the main table governs the whole VPC
choices.why: An explicit association overrides the main table, so three subnets ignore it.

prompt: Which fix does the lesson call the one that lasts, once the stray route is deleted?
hint: Privacy should be written down, not inherited.

choices.text: Renaming the subnet to `records-private`
choices.why: A name decides nothing.

choices.text: Giving the records subnet a table of its own, and leaving the main table with `local` only
choices.why: Right. The next edit to the main table then reaches only subnets nobody has thought about.

choices.text: Detaching the internet gateway from the VPC
choices.why: That takes the booking site off the internet too.

choices.text: A network ACL on the subnet
choices.why: A useful second layer, but it leaves the subnet following whatever the main table says next.

prompt: A subnet with no explicit association follows the VPC's ___ route table.
hint: AWS creates it with the VPC.

prompt: What outbound rule does a security group have when AWS creates it?
hint: Read before writing anything.

choices.text: HTTPS only, to AWS's own addresses
choices.why: No such default exists.

choices.text: Everything within the VPC's own range, and nothing beyond it
choices.why: That is the rule the lesson wrote for the database, not the default.

choices.text: None: outbound traffic is denied until a rule allows it
choices.why: That is the inbound side. Outbound starts with everything allowed.

choices.text: All protocols to `0.0.0.0/0`
choices.why: Right: protocol `-1` to every address, which the capture printed.

prompt: A database sits in a private subnet with a NAT gateway for updates. Nobody can connect to it from the internet. Can it send the table it holds to a server on the internet?
hint: Which direction does NAT allow?

choices.text: No, NAT only forwards traffic to AWS services
choices.why: NAT forwards to any address; that is how the updates arrive.

choices.text: Only if somebody first opens an inbound port for the reply
choices.why: Replies to an outbound connection come back through the NAT and the stateful group without any inbound rule.

choices.text: No, a private subnet cannot reach the internet
choices.why: With a NAT gateway it can open any outbound connection.

choices.text: Yes, unless the security group's outbound rules stop it
choices.why: Right. NAT lets connections out and says nothing about what goes out.

prompt: After the database's outbound rule is narrowed to `10.20.0.0/16`, a web server sends it a query. Does the answer get back?
hint: Security groups remember connections.

choices.text: Yes, because security groups are stateful
choices.why: Right: the reply is let out whatever the outbound rules say, and the web subnet is inside `10.20.0.0/16` anyway.

choices.text: No, a reply needs its own outbound rule
choices.why: That is how a stateless network ACL behaves, not a security group.

choices.text: Only if the web server's group allows inbound from the database
choices.why: The reply belongs to a connection the web server opened; it needs no inbound rule.

prompt: Match each outbound control to what it filters on.
hint: The table at the end of the section.

pairs.left: a proxy the machines go through

pairs.right: domain lists, inspected in the network

right_distractors: the user who started the process

prompt: The clinic's payment server needs to reach one payment provider. Which outbound policy does the lesson's reasoning favour?
hint: Whose list contains the server a thief set up yesterday?

choices.text: A security group rule allowing `0.0.0.0/0` on port 443 only
choices.why: Port 443 to everywhere is most of the internet, including a thief's server.

choices.text: A block list of known malicious domains, updated daily
choices.why: Nobody's block list contains yesterday's server; it is the weak version.

choices.text: An allow list naming the payment provider's host
choices.why: Right. The few destinations the workload needs, and nothing else.

choices.text: No outbound control, since the provider's addresses change too often to write down
choices.why: That is why the control filters on the host name rather than the address.

prompt: Which services can a gateway endpoint reach?
hint: Two, and both are storage.

choices.text: Every AWS service in the region
choices.why: That is closer to interface endpoints, which are billed.

choices.text: Any service published with AWS PrivateLink
choices.why: PrivateLink is what interface endpoints are built on.

choices.text: S3 alone
choices.why: DynamoDB too.

choices.text: S3 and DynamoDB
choices.why: Right. Every other service needs an interface endpoint.

prompt: After the gateway endpoint was created, what new route appeared in the records subnet's table?
hint: Its destination is not an address range.

choices.text: A `pl-` prefix list, to the `vpce-` endpoint
choices.why: Right. The prefix list is S3's set of addresses in São Paulo, kept up to date by AWS.

choices.text: None; a gateway endpoint works through DNS, without routes
choices.why: That describes an interface endpoint's private DNS. A gateway endpoint is a route.

choices.text: A route to the internet gateway for S3's addresses
choices.why: The whole point is that the path never leaves the VPC.

choices.text: `0.0.0.0/0` to the endpoint
choices.why: That would send everything to S3; the route is narrower.

prompt: Why did the database's security group need one more outbound rule after the endpoint existed?
hint: Where are S3's addresses?

choices.text: The route table needs a matching security group entry for every route
choices.why: Routes and security groups are independent controls; that is why the lesson has two.

choices.text: Endpoints refuse traffic from groups with no rule naming them
choices.why: The endpoint does not look at the group; the group looks at the destination.

choices.text: Because S3's addresses are outside `10.20.0.0/16`, the only range the group allowed out
choices.why: Right, so the rule names the same prefix list, on port 443.

prompt: A credential is stolen from the records database host. With the endpoint policy and the bucket policy of the lesson in place, which of these does AWS refuse, by its documentation? Choose all that apply.
hint: One policy narrows where the VPC's requests go; the other narrows where the bucket's come from.

choices.text: Writing the nightly backup to `clinic-records` from the database host
choices.why: That is the path both policies exist to allow.

choices.text: Any request to S3 from the database host at all
choices.why: The backup still goes through; only other buckets are out of reach.

choices.text: Copying the records to a bucket of the thief's, through the endpoint
choices.why: Right. The endpoint policy names `clinic-records` alone.

choices.text: Reading `clinic-records` with the stolen key from the thief's own laptop
choices.why: Right. The request did not come through the endpoint, and the bucket's explicit `Deny` wins.

prompt: What did the lab show about the bucket policy with `aws:SourceVpce`?
hint: Lesson 1's table says what moto does with conditions.

choices.text: That moto rejected it as malformed
choices.why: It accepted it and returned it intact.

choices.text: That it locked the administrators out of the bucket, as the warning says it can
choices.why: That is AWS's documented risk; moto applies no condition, so nobody was locked out.

choices.text: That it refused a request from outside the endpoint
choices.why: moto ignores conditions; no such refusal was produced.

choices.text: That moto stored it, with the endpoint's id in the condition
choices.why: Right. Its effect on AWS is from AWS's documentation, not a run.

prompt: Why does `exposure.py` read the main table's associations as well as the explicit ones?
hint: Which subnet did caio expose?

choices.text: To list the VPCs
choices.why: The VPC id is on every table already.

choices.text: boto3 refuses to describe a subnet unless its main table is fetched first
choices.why: boto3 has no such rule; the script would run and be wrong.

choices.text: So that subnets with no table of their own are judged too
choices.why: Right. Without them caio's subnet would be missed: inheritance is where the first section's mistake lived.

choices.text: Because only the main table can hold a route to an internet gateway
choices.why: The web subnet's own table holds one.

prompt: How many findings did the first run of `exposure.py` print?
hint: Count the lines under the command.

prompt: The checker printed `OPEN TO EVERYONE ... clinic-web ports 443-443`. What should happen to that finding?
hint: A finding is a question, not a verdict.

choices.text: Revoke the rule at once, since nothing should be open to everybody
choices.why: A public booking site is supposed to answer everybody on HTTPS; revoking it takes the site down.

choices.text: Recognise it as intended, because that is what the booking site is for
choices.why: Right. Only somebody who knows what the clinic meant can tell the intended from the mistake.

choices.text: Ignore the checker, since it reports things that are fine
choices.why: The same run found the SSH rule, which was the real fault.

choices.text: Move the site to port 8443, which the checker treats differently
choices.why: The checker flags any port open to everybody; a different number hides nothing.

prompt: Which of these can `exposure.py`, as written, not see? Choose all that apply.
hint: The last paragraph of the section.

choices.text: A subnet that follows a main table with a route to an internet gateway
choices.why: That is the case the main-table part was written for.

choices.text: A subnet in another region
choices.why: Right. It reads one region, and the account has 38.

choices.text: Whether any packet actually reached the open port
choices.why: Right. Configuration says what is allowed; flow logs say what happened.

choices.text: A security group rule admitting `0.0.0.0/0`
choices.why: That is exactly what its last part looks for.

choices.text: A network ACL
choices.why: Right. It never reads them.

prompt: Which question does a flow log answer that the configuration cannot?
hint: Allowed against happened.

choices.text: Which connections actually happened
choices.why: Right. One line per conversation, if it was on at the time.

choices.text: Who changed the security group
choices.why: That is a record of API calls, lesson 15's subject.

choices.text: Which ports are open to everybody
choices.why: Configuration answers that; the checker did.

choices.text: What a session typed once it was connected
choices.why: A flow log records conversations, not contents.

prompt: A flow log line reads `... 203.0.113.50 10.20.1.10 51544 22 6 ... ACCEPT OK`. What does it record?
hint: Source before destination; `6` is a protocol number.

choices.text: The web server opening an outbound connection to `203.0.113.50` on port 22, which was then accepted
choices.why: The source is `203.0.113.50`; the destination port is 22 on the web server.

choices.text: A TCP connection from `203.0.113.50` to the web server's SSH port, accepted
choices.why: Right, and the line an investigation of the open port is looking for.

choices.text: A refused attempt on port 22
choices.why: The action is `ACCEPT`.

choices.text: Six SSH sessions
choices.why: `6` is the protocol number, TCP.

prompt: Which of these are true of VPC flow logs, by the lesson? Choose all that apply.
hint: Four things a flow log does not say.

choices.text: They are off until somebody turns them on
choices.why: Right, and the morning after an incident is too late.

choices.text: They carry the payload of each packet
choices.why: Conversations, not contents.

choices.text: They aggregate traffic over windows, up to ten minutes by default
choices.why: Right: counts per window, not a timeline to the second.

choices.text: moto wrote records into the bucket in the lab
choices.why: The bucket stayed empty; moto carries no traffic.

choices.text: Requests to the instance metadata address are left out
choices.why: Right, by AWS's documentation.

prompt: Put the steps of the route fix in the order the lesson took them.
hint: The proof comes last, and it is the first question asked again.
items: find the main table and read its routes
delete the `0.0.0.0/0` route from the main table
create a private table for the records subnet
associate the records subnet with it
ask for the records subnet's routes again
trap: Associating before creating is impossible; stopping before the last step leaves the fix unproved.

prompt: In a flow log record, protocol number `6` is ___.
hint: UDP is 17.
